Frail
frāl
adj. (weak, easily broken; what David asked to be taught about himself)
From Latin fragilis, breakable, from frangere, to break. Psalm 39:4 uses it for Hebrew chadel, ceasing or transient — and David asks to be shown it, which makes frailty a lesson rather than merely a condition.

Biblical Definition

David makes a request that few would make: “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am” (Psalm 39:4). He is not asking for a date; he is asking to be taught the fact he already knows and does not feel. Frailty is the one universal condition that men successfully forget, and David treats the forgetting as the danger. The figures Scripture gives are agricultural and brief: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psalm 103:15), and the prophet is given the same word as his commission: “The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6). James turns it on the businessman's calendar: “Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (James 4:14). None of these passages ends in despair. Isaiah 40 goes straight on to say that the word of our God shall stand for ever, and Psalm 103 follows the grass with the mercy of the LORD from everlasting to everlasting.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines frail as weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed; perishable; not firm or durable.

expand to see more

FRAIL, a. [L. fragilis, from frango, to break.] Weak; infirm; liable to fail and decay; subject to casualties; easily destroyed; perishable; not firm or durable.

FRAIL, a. Weak in mind or resolution; liable to error or deception.

FRAILTY, n. Weakness of resolution; infirmity; liableness to be deceived or seduced.

FRAILTY, n. Frailness; infirmity of body; instability; liableness to decay and perish.

VAPOR, n. [L. vapor.] In a general sense, an invisible elastic fluid, rendered aeriform by heat; steam; that which is fleeting and unsubstantial.

Key Scripture

Psalm 39:4 — "LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is; that I may know how frail I am."

Psalm 103:15 — "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth."

Isaiah 40:6 — "The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:"

James 4:14 — "Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away."

Modern Corruption

Mortality is managed rather than known — postponed by medicine, hidden by the funeral trade, deferred by the calendar — and the instruction David asked for is unavailable.

expand to see more

The modern arrangement is not that men deny death but that they are never taught it. The dying are moved out of the house, the dead are handled by professionals, and the word itself is replaced. What David asks for in Psalm 39:4 — to be made to know the measure of his days — a whole civilization is organized to prevent. Moses prayed the same: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Wisdom in Scripture has a prerequisite, and the prerequisite is a true estimate of one's own length.

The opposite error is to make frailty the last word, which Scripture never does. Every passage that calls man grass has a clause after it. Isaiah 40:6 is followed by the word of our God shall stand for ever, which Peter quotes and applies to the gospel preached. Psalm 103 follows the flower of the field with mercy from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear Him. James 4:14 is followed by the right sentence to say about tomorrow: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. Frailty known drives a man out of himself, which is exactly where it was meant to send him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chadel (H2310), transient, ceasing; chatsir (H2682), grass; tsits (H6731), a flower; Greek atmis (G822), a vapour.

expand to see more

Hebrew chadel (H2310) — frail, fleeting; Psalm 39:4, what David asked to be taught.

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass; Psalm 103:15 and Isaiah 40:6.

Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom; the flower of the field that fades.

Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour, mist; James 4:14, appearing a little time.

Hebrew manah (H4487) — to number, appoint; Psalm 90:12, so teach us to number our days.

Usage

"“That I may know how frail I am” — a fact asked for as a lesson."

"“All flesh is grass” — and the next clause is the word that stands."

"“It is even a vapour” — said to men making a two-year plan."
